Nature: it is political science (what people DO) + political philosophy (what they OUGHT to do); functions = describe, criticise, reconstruct.
Relevance: not dead — it guides action (reform/revolution); without it politics is ‘left to the ignorant’ (Held); hence Plamenatz’s ‘arduous calling’.

Q — Discuss the significance of the normative approach to political theory, situating it among the traditional approaches. (UPSC 2020)
An ‘approach’ = criteria for selecting which questions and data to study (Van Dyke); traditional approaches came before behaviouralism.
Normative/philosophical (Plato, Strauss): asks what OUGHT to be — justice, rights; it clarifies concepts and sets standards of right/wrong.
Other traditional: historical (Sabine — ‘child of his times’), empirical (Aristotle — ‘what is’), legal-institutional (Wheare, Dicey).
Significance: keeps values central — science gives means, philosophy gives ends; no single approach suffices.

Q — Examine the importance of the behavioural approach in political theory. What led to its decline? (UPSC 2021)
Behaviouralism = make politics a science: study actual behaviour (voting), use data, stay value-neutral.
Roots: Wallas & Bentley (1908), Merriam (Chicago School), Catlin; systematised in Easton’s 8 tenets.
Importance: arrested PT’s decline; pioneered electoral studies; made comparative politics a major field.
Decline: dropping values (Strauss critique) + obsession with technique made it irrelevant to 1960s crises → post-behaviouralism.

Q — Comment on the post-behavioural approach. “It is a synthesis of tradition and behaviouralism.” (UPSC 2016)
Post-behaviouralism (Easton, 1969 ‘Credo of Relevance’): technique is fine, but research must be RELEVANT and value-laden.
Two watchwords: Action + Relevance; “better to be vague than non-relevantly precise.”
It is a synthesis: traditionalism = thesis, behaviouralism = antithesis, post-behaviouralism = synthesis — NOT a rejection of behaviouralism.
It restored values without dropping science → led to the resurgence of political theory.

Q — “Political theory is dead.” Critically examine the debate on the decline of political theory. What, according to David Easton, were its causes? (UPSC 2018)
1950s claim: classical PT is ‘dead’ — too speculative, out of touch (Easton, The Political System, 1953).
Easton’s 4 causes: historicism, moral relativism, method-over-purpose, hyper-factualism.
Others: Cobban (lost in both capitalism & communism), Lipset (‘good society achieved’), Strauss (positivism ignores values).
Conclude: not death but an eclipse of the normative side — soon revived.

The ‘decline’ was not the death of political theory but a temporary eclipse of its normative-philosophical side by positivism. As even Cobban admitted, ‘all was not yet lost’ — and Easton himself soon launched the post-behavioural revival.
Q — Comment on the resurgence of political theory. Account for its revival since the 1970s. (UPSC 2019)
From the 1970s, PT bounced back — values returned and science & philosophy were reconciled.
Trigger: the post-behavioural turn (1969) — applied science + relevance.
Revival of philosophy: Germino (Beyond Ideology) — Oakeshott, Arendt, Strauss, Rawls.
Convergence: Rawls uses method for justice; science = means, philosophy = ends.

contentText: Syllabus — Political Theory: meaning and approaches. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 1) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  meaning, nature, scope and contents of political theory; political theory as history / philosophy / science; the debate on the decline and resurgence of political theory; and approaches — Traditional (philosophical/normative, historical, empirical, legal, institutional), Modern (behavioural, post-behavioural, systems) and Contemporary/Other (postmodern, textual & contextual, deconstruction). Must-know thinkers:  Sabine, Catlin, Hacker, Leo Strauss, Dante Germino, David Easton, Alfred Cobban, Lipset, David Held, John Plamenatz, Van Dyke, Wallas, Bentley, Merriam, Skinner & Pocock, Derrida, Skocpol. PYQ trend:  near-annual. Decline (2018) & Resurgence (2019); Behavioural (2021), Post-Behavioural (2016), Normative (2020) and Systems (2022) approaches; nature/relevance of political theory (Plamenatz, 2014). Master Questions Q — “Political theory is not an escape mechanism but an arduous calling.” (Plamenatz) Examine the meaning, nature and relevance of political theory. (UPSC 2014) Gist — the spine to recall Define: political theory = the science + philosophy of everything ‘political’ (Sabine); a mix of history, philosophy and science. Nature: it is political science (what people DO) + political philosophy (what they OUGHT to do); functions = describe, criticise, reconstruct. Relevance: not dead — it guides action (reform/revolution); without it politics is ‘left to the ignorant’ (Held); hence Plamenatz’s ‘arduous calling’. Conclude with the synthesis of facts + values; example = Rawls. Model Answer Political theory is the systematic study of everything ‘political’ — the state, power, justice and the good society.  George Sabine  calls it “anything about politics or relevant to politics.” It is neither pure philosophy nor pure science, but a mix of both together with history. It is  history  in so far as it rests on facts,  philosophy  in so far as it judges values, and  science  in so far as it explains — so a theorist is ‘part historian, part philosopher, part scientist’.  Catlin  and  Hacker  show that political theory = political science (what people actually DO) + political philosophy (what they OUGHT to do), performing three functions:  description, criticism and reconstruction . It must stay distinct from ideology: a theory is dispassionate, whereas an ideology defends a particular structure of power. Its relevance is real —  David Held  warns that without political theory, “politics is left to the ignorant and self-interested.” This is why  Plamenatz  called it “not an escape mechanism but an arduous calling” — a demanding, morally serious vocation. Conclusion.  Political theory is far from dead; it survives as a practical, action-guiding activity, a synthesis of facts and values.  Rawls’s   A Theory of Justice (1971)  shows how it blends moral reasoning with rigorous method. Q — Discuss the significance of the normative approach to political theory, situating it among the traditional approaches. (UPSC 2020) Gist — the spine to recall An ‘approach’ = criteria for selecting which questions and data to study (Van Dyke); traditional approaches came before behaviouralism. Normative/philosophical (Plato, Strauss): asks what OUGHT to be — justice, rights; it clarifies concepts and sets standards of right/wrong. Other traditional: historical (Sabine — ‘child of his times’), empirical (Aristotle — ‘what is’), legal-institutional (Wheare, Dicey). Significance: keeps values central — science gives means, philosophy gives ends; no single approach suffices. Model Answer An ‘approach’ is, in  Van Dyke’s  words, the  “criteria of selection”  that decide which problems and data we study. Among the traditional approaches, the normative (philosophical) approach is the most enduring. Normative approach  ( Plato, Leo Strauss ): prescriptive; deals with justice, rights and liberty. It does two things — clarifies political concepts, and sets ‘standards of right and wrong’ to judge institutions and laws. Strauss held that facts and values are both indispensable. Other traditional approaches:  the  historical  ( Sabine, Machiavelli ) studies politics through its past — Laski: “every thinker is the child of his times”; the  empirical  ( Aristotle, Locke ) describes ‘what is’, not ‘what ought to be’; the  legal-institutional  ( Wheare, Dicey ) studies law, the constitution and government machinery. Significance & critique.  The normative approach keeps values at the centre — empirical study ‘strengthens our means’, but we need philosophy ‘to determine our ends’. Critics call it ‘arm-chair theory’, yet it revived through the Frankfurt School, communitarianism and multiculturalism. Conclusion.  No single approach suffices; a combination is needed.  Rawls’s  revival of normative justice in the 1970s proves its lasting significance. Q — Examine the importance of the behavioural approach in political theory. What led to its decline? (UPSC 2021) Gist — the spine to recall Behaviouralism = make politics a science: study actual behaviour (voting), use data, stay value-neutral. Roots: Wallas & Bentley (1908), Merriam (Chicago School), Catlin; systematised in Easton’s 8 tenets. Importance: arrested PT’s decline; pioneered electoral studies; made comparative politics a major field. Decline: dropping values (Strauss critique) + obsession with technique made it irrelevant to 1960s crises → post-behaviouralism. Model Answer Behaviouralism was the attempt to turn politics into a science by studying how people actually behave, using data and remaining value-neutral. It flourished among American scholars after the Second World War, though it began with  Graham Wallas  and  Arthur Bentley  (1908). Its foundations were  David Easton’s   eight tenets  — regularities, systematisation, technique, measurement, verification, integration, value-neutrality and pure science. Pioneers included  Charles Merriam  (the Chicago School) and  G.E.G. Catlin  (a value-free ‘science of power’). Importance:  it arrested the decline of the discipline, pioneered electoral-behaviour studies (aiding party strategy), and made comparative politics a major field by showing that in developing countries ‘text differs from context’. Decline:  traditionalists like  Leo Strauss  attacked value-neutrality — ignoring values, he said, is like “making no difference between pure and dirty water.” By chasing technique it lost relevance;  Easton  himself admitted scholars sat in ‘ivory towers’. The social upheavals of the 1950s-60s exposed this, triggering the post-behavioural revolution of 1969. Conclusion.  Behaviouralism made political science rigorous, but its neglect of values caused a ‘second decline’, out of which post-behaviouralism emerged as a corrective. Q — Comment on the post-behavioural approach. “It is a synthesis of tradition and behaviouralism.” (UPSC 2016) Gist — the spine to recall Post-behaviouralism (Easton, 1969 ‘Credo of Relevance’): technique is fine, but research must be RELEVANT and value-laden. Two watchwords: Action + Relevance; “better to be vague than non-relevantly precise.” It is a synthesis: traditionalism = thesis, behaviouralism = antithesis, post-behaviouralism = synthesis — NOT a rejection of behaviouralism. It restored values without dropping science → led to the resurgence of political theory. Model Answer Post-behaviouralism was launched by  David Easton  in his 1969 presidential address, the  ‘Credo of Relevance’ . It grew out of dissatisfaction with behaviouralism’s neglect of values and social relevance. Its core slogan was “it is better to be vague than non-relevantly precise.” Easton called for a  ‘creative theory’  built on two parameters —  Action  and  Relevance . Its features: it does not reject values but invites them; theory must help solve social crises; political science is an  applied , not a pure, science; and the intellectual’s responsibility is greater than the natural scientist’s. It is best understood as a  synthesis  — traditionalism (thesis) and behaviouralism (antithesis) resolved into post-behaviouralism (synthesis). Crucially, it does NOT reject behaviouralism; it keeps its methods but adds relevance and values. Conclusion.  By restoring the normative dimension without abandoning scientific method, post-behaviouralism reconciled facts and values and paved the way for the resurgence of political theory.  Rawls’s   A Theory of Justice (1971)  reflects this new ‘creative’ spirit. Q — “Political theory is dead.” Critically examine the debate on the decline of political theory. What, according to David Easton, were its causes? (UPSC 2018) Gist — the spine to recall 1950s claim: classical PT is ‘dead’ — too speculative, out of touch (Easton, The Political System, 1953). Easton’s 4 causes: historicism, moral relativism, method-over-purpose, hyper-factualism. Others: Cobban (lost in both capitalism & communism), Lipset (‘good society achieved’), Strauss (positivism ignores values). Conclude: not death but an eclipse of the normative side — soon revived. Model Answer In the 1950s the ‘new science of politics’ declared traditional political theory to be in decline.  David Easton , in  The Political System (1953) , dismissed it as “mere speculation,” out of touch with political reality. Easton gave  four causes  of the decline:  historicism  (obsession with century-old ideas made the discipline ‘parasitic’);  moral relativism  (values excluded to make politics value-neutral);  confusion of science and theory  (method given primacy over purpose); and  hyper-factualism  (an obsession with facts, producing ‘theoretical malnutrition and a surfeit of facts’). Others joined in:  Alfred Cobban  said theory had lost relevance in both capitalist and communist systems;  Seymour Lipset  claimed the search for the ‘good society’ had ended; and  Leo Strauss  argued that positivism ignored normative issues and ‘obliterated the distinction between men and brutes’. Conclusion.  The ‘decline’ was not the death of political theory but a temporary eclipse of its normative-philosophical side by positivism. As even Cobban admitted, ‘all was not yet lost’ — and Easton himself soon launched the post-behavioural revival. Q — Comment on the resurgence of political theory. Account for its revival since the 1970s. (UPSC 2019) Gist — the spine to recall From the 1970s, PT bounced back — values returned and science & philosophy were reconciled. Trigger: the post-behavioural turn (1969) — applied science + relevance. Revival of philosophy: Germino (Beyond Ideology) — Oakeshott, Arendt, Strauss, Rawls. Convergence: Rawls uses method for justice; science = means, philosophy = ends. Model Answer After being written off in the 1950s, political theory staged a strong resurgence from the 1970s, marked by the return of values and the reconciliation of facts and values. The turning point was  Easton’s  post-behavioural ‘Credo of Relevance’ (1969), which converted political science from a ‘pure’ to an ‘applied’ science concerned with real problems.  Dante Germino , in  Beyond Ideology: The Revival of Political Theory , showed the grand tradition reviving through  Michael Oakeshott, Hannah Arendt, Leo Strauss and John Rawls . Science and philosophy converged:  Karl Popper  drew value conclusions,  John Rawls  used an empirical device (the ‘original position’) for his principles of justice, and  C.B. Macpherson  challenged the empirical theory of democracy. New concerns — feminism, human rights, environmentalism — reopened value-judgment. Conclusion.  It is now accepted that political science gives us the ‘means’ while political philosophy determines our ‘ends’ — the two are complementary.  Rawls’s   A Theory of Justice (1971)  is the finest fruit of this resurgence, confirming that political theory is ‘not dead’. Q — Comment on the systems approach to the study of politics, and situate it among the other modern and contemporary approaches. (UPSC 2022) Gist — the spine to recall Systems approach (Easton): politics = input → conversion → output → feedback; the ‘authoritative allocation of values’. Strength: a holistic, comparative, self-regulating model of politics. Critique: too abstract, status-quoist, Eurocentric, ignores power and the individual. Other approaches: textual vs contextual (Skinner), Derrida’s deconstruction — no single approach suffices. Model Answer The systems approach, pioneered by  David Easton , was the most influential modern attempt to build a general theory of the political process. Easton treats the ‘political system’ as the mechanism for the  ‘authoritative allocation of values’ . Politics works as a cycle:  inputs  (society’s demands and supports) →  conversion  inside the system →  outputs  (decisions and policies) →  feedback , which generates fresh demands and keeps the system in balance. Strength:  a holistic, comparative and self-regulating model.  Weaknesses:  it is too abstract,  status-quoist  (it favours stability over change), Eurocentric, and neglects power and the individual. Other approaches:  the  textual  approach reads classics literally, while the  contextual  approach (the Cambridge School —  Skinner, Pocock ) reads them in their linguistic context.  Jacques Derrida’s   deconstruction  holds that “no meaning is ultimate — every understanding can be a misunderstanding.” Conclusion.  The sheer range of approaches shows that no single one can capture politics fully; as  Theda Skocpol  urged in ‘bringing the state back in’, a combination is needed to keep the discipline relevant.
